member of the commission. − madam president, it is a great pleasure and honour for me to address the european parliament today for the vote of consent to the stabilisation and association agreement with the republic of serbia. i would also like to express my warm gratitude to the rapporteur for serbia, jelko kacin, for his report on the european integration process of serbia. the stabilisation and association agreement is a major step forward for serbia on its path towards the european union. the fundamental objective of this agreement is to pave the way for further european integration and reforms and to prepare serbia for european union membership. this important milestone will serve as an encouragement for serbia, as it has renewed its efforts to promote reconciliation in the region. the stabilisation and association agreement sets up a comprehensive institutional framework through the saa council and saa committee, a renewed framework for political dialogue and a network of subcommittees extensively covering most european union policy areas. naturally, it also establishes a specific body between this house and the serbian parliament, the joint parliamentary committee. from an economic standpoint, the saa foresees the gradual establishment of a free trade zone and the gradual integration of serbia into the european union’s internal market, thus bringing economic benefits for both the european union and serbia. as was the case in central europe in the 1990s, the agreement will boost investment, in particular for indirect investments. it will make a key contribution to the growth of the serbian economy and help serbia move towards a functioning market economy. the benefits of this agreement for the european union are equally significant. serbia’s market has now been opened up to european union exporters. previously relatively high tariffs will be totally dismantled within a couple of years, with the exception of a few very sensitive agricultural products. furthermore, by gradually integrating serbia into the internal market, conditions for investors will become more stable and predictable. rules on competition and state aid are aligned to those of the european union. protection of intellectual property rights is also gradually being brought up to european union standards. the sizeable serbian public procurement market is also being progressively opened up to european bidders. forging closer ties with serbia entails a number of other advantages for the european union in particular, as it will facilitate cooperation in the areas of justice, freedom and security, the environment, transport and customs, to mention just a few. it therefore helps make the european union’s policy in south-east europe more credible and effective. finally, it is particularly noteworthy that serbia brought forward the implementation of the interim agreement. it officially entered into force in february 2010, but serbia decided to apply it shortly after it was signed in april 2008. serbia has thereby demonstrated a commitment to its economic integration with the european union and has so far established a positive track record. since 14 june 2010, when the council decided to launch the ratification process for the agreement, nine member states have notified ratification and two more have secured the approval of their parliaments. today’s vote by the european parliament should therefore provide additional impetus for this process thanks to the unanimous support from across the political groups. i hope that ratification by the other member states will follow soon. let me conclude by focusing on the motion for a resolution on the european integration process of serbia as a well-prepared contribution to today’s political debate. i am therefore grateful to the rapporteur, jelko kacin. the resolution sends serbia both a message of support for enhancing eu-serbia relations, and a message of expectation in relation to the key challenges on serbia’s path to european union membership. this is particularly timely in the context of the preparations of the opinion on serbia’s membership application. i was in belgrade last november to hand over a detailed questionnaire to the prime minister and the deputy prime minister for european integration. the serbian authorities are currently working hard on their replies, which we expect by the end of the month. i am encouraged by the serbian government’s adoption on 30 december of an action plan as a follow-up to the commission’s progress report. the commission will thoroughly analyse the replies to the questionnaires and the steps taken by the serbian authorities in the coming months to complete its assessment with a view to issuing the opinion in the second half of 2011. as my hungarian colleague said, 2011 is an important year for serbia: a year of demanding challenges as well as a year of opportunities. the path has been set and the objectives are well known, yet it is up to serbia to walk down that path, fulfil the required criteria, and, once ready, engage in the negotiation process with the european union. i am convinced that, with our joint support, serbia will continue to make the right european choices and move ahead in its integration efforts. this will deliver a positive message for the whole region at a time when we need to reaffirm its european perspective in order to consolidate peace and foster economic prosperity in the western balkans.

president of the commission. − we are pushing for that. we are trying to put the issue forward for the next european council. energy efficiency is still lagging behind, as you said. i am not happy with the situation and the commission intends to reverse it. energy efficiency is now an integral part of the headline target of the eu 2020 strategy. we are currently in talks with the member states to establish national targets to underpin this objective. we have already estimated that, with existing policies and measures, the saving by 2020 would be no more than 10%. however, the combined national indicative targets emerging in the europe 2020 discussions give a result that is clearly more ambitious than that, but still likely to be well below the 20%. that is why we intend to follow a two-step approach, by closely monitoring the progress made with the implementation of national targets defined in europe 2020, and reviewing this progress in 2013. if these reviews show that our target of 20% is unlikely to be achieved, the commission will consider proposing legally binding national targets for 2020.
president of the commission. − mr president, first of all let me say that the commissioner is the one who is proposing this additional approach to energy efficiency and i fully trust that he is doing his best to achieve that goal. we are also trying to link this energy issue to other policy objectives like the fight against climate change. that said, we believe this is not just a matter of setting targets, it is also about work in the member states, and so we believe that it is better for the member states to establish their own national targets and then we shall see. if they are on track, great. if not, we will at least propose binding legislation. but to achieve success it is sometimes better to start with a kind of voluntary target. at least, that is what we have done in the past and it has proved to be the right approach. we do not exclude – quite the contrary – a possible need for binding targets for each country, but let us also give the member states ownership of this policy and see how they develop their strategy.

vice-president of the commission. − the commission’s communication on europe 2020 and its communication on the digital agenda for europe set the objective of bringing basic broadband to all europeans by 2013 and seek to ensure that by 2020 all europeans have access to much higher internet speeds of above 30 megabytes per second and that 50% or more of european households have subscribed to internet connection above 100 megabytes per second. mr president, the commission is aware that without strong public intervention there is a risk of sub-optimal roll-out with fast proven networks concentrated in high-density zones and with remote and rural areas lagging behind. that would also have negative consequences on educational systems and integration of information and communication technology in education. the latest eu-wide data shows that only 67% of schools have broadband access and that there were large disparities between member states and between densely and thinly populated areas, 73.7% and 60.6% respectively. to avoid the risk of a sub-optimal roll-out, the commission has adopted a broadband package outlining a common framework within both national and regional policies, which should be developed to meet the targets. those policies should, in particular, lower the cost of broadband deployment in the entire eu territory by ensuring proper planning and coordination and reducing administrative burdens. the commission has already acted to increase investment in remote areas and regions within the framework of the eu cohesion policy with the programming of about eur 2.3 billion in the period 2007-2013. the commission’s communication on a european economic recovery plan also enabled the programming of eur 360 million in broadband measures for rural areas through the european agricultural fund for rural development. in its programme package the commission announced that it will reinforce and rationalise the funding of high-speed broadband through eu instruments by 2014 and explore how to attract capital for broadband investment through credit enhancement backed by the european investment bank and the eu funds. an ec-eib proposal on the issue is expected in 2011. another pillar from the digital agenda is dedicated to digital skills. here we propose for instance to consider digital literacy and competences as a priority for the european social fund regulation in the next programming period and to identify digital competences as a supplement to europass to ensure their transparency. education, as you are aware, is crucial to the development of digital competences in our society and we agree that without appropriate investment some regions may lag behind. the latest eu-wide data – i am talking about 2006 – shows that only 67% of schools had broadband access and that there were large disparities between eu member states and between densely and thinly populated areas. we are about to launch a new survey on schools and the results will be available at the end of this year.

in writing. i voted today in favour of the joint resolution on intercountry adoption in the eu, which aims to improve the system of adoption between member states and to establish safeguards to ensure that adoption is in the best interests of the child with full respect for his or her fundamental rights. the resolution emphasizes the following: • the creation of a european strategy on adoption, which will define the rules for adoption from the poorest to the most developed countries and will make it possible to monitor the progress of each child placed under international adoption arrangements by means of periodic reports submitted by the competent national authorities in the children's country of origin. • simplification of the procedures required for adoption and reduction of red tape. • reducing the time spent by children in institutions and orphanages. • priority in national adoptions. (iii) the elimination of the unfair practices of child exploitation and trafficking for the purpose of adoption.

in writing. i voted in favour of the report on the european alzheimer's disease initiative, as it will help to improve the quality of life of patients and their families and reduce disparities between member states in terms of prevention, access to treatment and provision of appropriate services to patients with dementia. in europe, 1.4 million citizens have some form of dementia, and over 8 million europeans aged between 30 and 99 suffer from neurodegenerative diseases - half of them have alzheimer's - and their number is expected to double every 20 years. the report seeks to improve the situation, with the main objectives of promoting early diagnosis and prevention and improving the quality of life of patients, solidarity and a uniform approach between the various countries, from research to medical care, and the promotion of the dignity of patients throughout their treatment.

vice-president of the commission. - mr president, i will try to be as precise as i was when i was a member of parliament. we are dealing with topics of great interest, in particular the european commission's desire to support the entrepreneurial spirit and improve the environment in which businesses, in particular small and medium-sized enterprises, operate by supporting them in accessing markets in third countries: i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. this is why the commission's review of the small business act for europe, adopted in 2008, is due to take place in the coming days. the principles and provisions of the small business act are fully consistent with the priorities of the europe 2020 strategy and their implementation at national level will be ensured through the support of all stakeholders. this means that all member states and business organisations will be involved in monitoring the results achieved. we want to ensure that the principles set out in the small business act, which aim to promote entrepreneurship and to eradicate the 'small' thinking in policy-making, are implemented at both community and national level. we have already introduced a test for small and mediumsized enterprises, which is intended to take greater account of the impact assessment procedure of the various policies and the constraints which restrict small and mediumsized enterprises. the review of the small business act will include measures to harmonise the use of this test and to improve the quality of assessments. in addition, all member states will be encouraged to follow the same approach in their national decision-making procedures. aware of the need to reduce administrative burdens and eliminate disparities at national level, we will indicate concrete actions - such as the creation of one-stop shops and the use of egovernment to accelerate the processes. the commission also organises exchanges of best practice between national administrations on specific topics. to stimulate the entrepreneurial spirit of young people and to promote crossborder business cooperation in europe, we have set up the erasmus programme for young entrepreneurs, also at the instigation of the european parliament, and the results have been positive. we therefore intend to try to give the project a legal basis by turning it from a pilot action into a permanent programme. we have also planned measures specifically for women entrepreneurs: we have a network today of 250 ambassadors from 22 european countries. i hope this network can be intensified. finally, we are working to create mentoring programmes for women entrepreneurs in at least 12 eu countries. as regards assistance to smes for export and investment outside the union, we launched a wide public consultation early last year on our intentions to strengthen support measures, the results of which will allow us to adapt the proposed guidelines to enhance support services for smes while ensuring an efficient use of public funds. we have already built up a solid experience in assisting the internationalisation of smes - member of the commission. − madam president, i would like to thank members for this very substantial, inspirational and stimulating discussion. i would like to answer all the major points that have been raised as questions or comments and observations concerning the annual growth survey, the economic semester and europe 2020 in general. the most important thing is that we get the picture right, both about the documents and also about the economic situation in the european union. the inconvenient truth is that europe is experiencing a recovery. last year we already had economic growth in the european union – but not in every member state – and that is where the second part of the inconvenient truth comes. we are experiencing a very fragile and divided recovery. the commission has looked at this situation very thoroughly and developed policies accordingly. we need to maintain and strengthen the recovery, and we have to address the current division. this will not, however, be possible without addressing the weaknesses that have been exposed by the crisis in economic and monetary union, which we will do by developing further the architecture of economic and monetary governance in the european union. that is where the complications begin and where it may be true that the priorities are not always immediately recognised by everyone. for us, economic growth is the priority and all other policies in this phase serve this. we need to strengthen growth and make it more robust, but in order to do this we need a greater level of financial stability, and for that we also need fiscal consolidation. it is inevitable that, in the coming years, fiscal consolidation will remain on the agenda in the interests of stabilisation and of being consistent with the kinds of cyclical intervention which the member states implemented against the recession in previous years. we need a smart consolidation which does not undermine demand in the economy and which preserves the integrity of the eu economy as a whole. this lesson has to be learned. this must begin by stabilising the euro. i could obviously use stronger expressions here, but let us just stick to this one. we need to stabilise the euro and economic and monetary union. the lesson we share is that, in order to do that, we need to strengthen the economic leg of this union and the economic leg of policy coordination at european level. let me just ask a question and leave it as a question on this. the question is whether the strengthening of the economic leg of governance can succeed without a collective effort on wages, on coordinating wage developments in the european union. when i say that, and when we include suggestions in this area in the annual growth survey, it does not mean that we would question the importance of the social dialogue – quite the contrary. we have praised countries with a tradition and culture of strong social partnership. we recognise that they suffered less from the crisis and, in particular, suffered fewer losses in terms of human resources. unemployment remained lower in these countries. we advocate the strengthening of social dialogue in other member states which have suffered more and which responded to the crisis with less flexibility than countries like germany, the netherlands or austria. we have also increased the level of social dialogue at european level. we recently held macroeconomic dialogue with the social partners and we will have a new tripartite social forum in march in order to enhance coordination and dialogue with the social partners. i would like to reject very categorically the notion that the commission is doing business as usual. in the last year the commission has introduced a number of qualitatively new initiatives. we are pursuing a robust agenda for financial regulation. commissioner barnier’s work should not be underestimated. as part of europe 2020, we outlined a new concept for industrial policy at european level which does much more for competitiveness and the sustainability of jobs in the european union. we are pursuing a number of innovative approaches to boost investment and to find funding for it. a group of commissioners has been working to develop innovative financial instruments. the first example of this is going to be an outline for supporting developing energy networks in europe. this is absolutely necessary in order to develop the energy markets and the necessary infrastructure that is vital for it. we have launched the microfinance facility. i am grateful to parliament and the council for the final consensus that made this possible last year. just last week i was present in the netherlands at the launch of the first eu-supported microfinance facility and there are more in the pipeline in order to support potential entrepreneurs, perhaps after the experience of being unemployed: women coming back to the labour market after childbirth or people who have already been working and want to seek a new form of enterprise beyond 50, or even 60. when we discuss employment policies – and a good example of this was a couple of weeks ago when the epsco council was hosted by the hungarian presidency in gödöllő – we focus on how to generate job-rich goals, but also on the groups in most difficulty. in this case i must mention in particular young people. youth unemployment is very dramatic in some member states. again we have to be aware of diversity. luckily, there are some member states where youth unemployment is low, but the european average is too high. in some member states, like spain and the baltics, it is at a tragic level. the governments have been alerted and a complex set of policies, from education to employment services and other types of measures, is required. but youth is not the only problem group. it is true that we have to do more with regard to the employment of older workers. that is why we designated 2012 the european year for active ageing. on the institutional questions concerning the employment guidelines – which i believe continue to be our focus and provide guidance and substance – there is a clear role for the european nor overruled by annual growth surveys. the guidelines provide long-term orientation, while the growth survey is an annual exercise that concerns its substance. but it is obviously true that the nrp multiannual financial framework negotiations. the eu budget also has to reflect 2020 priorities and we will keep parliament informed about the preparation of the national reform programme as the country-specific recommendations develop. it is clear that there is concern at this early stage about the future of europe 2020. in a way, a spectre is haunting europe 2020: that of the lisbon strategy. i have had many opportunities in this house to discuss why we believe there is a much better chance, through a more focused system of targets and also a more focused system of reporting and in writing. i voted against the report on the green paper on european pension schemes. the report clearly promotes the anti-social policies of the european union and the neoliberal leveling of social rights. the text provides for an increase in the retirement age of european workers and for the linking of this age to life expectancy. european workers, having paid for the bank bailouts and subjected to exhaustive austerity measures, are again forced to pay the consequences of a crisis, one they did not create, by working longer hours and receiving reduced pensions. the left group, in its alternative resolution, which unfortunately was not adopted, opposed the green paper on pensions and pointed out the possibility of improving pensions and retirement conditions for the benefit of workers. this is possible without raising the age limits but through increased labour rights, especially for young people, better wages and at the same time higher taxation on financial capital and financial transactions.

level. innovative financial instruments can play a key role in addressing these challenges, as they can make a decisive contribution to generating significant new revenue for national budgets and the community budget. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. innovation in finance is not just about finding new resources; it is equally important to pave the way for a gradual change in the current tax model, where the main burden of taxation and more generally of financing the economy has traditionally been borne by sectors such as labour, enterprises and productive investment. the important added value of innovative financial instruments, the double benefit, as we say, is that in addition to revenue they can also have a strong regulatory role: to discourage practices and behaviours that are harmful, whether we are talking about the financial sector or the environment and its protection. the report covers four main thematic areas: taxation of the financial sector, eurobonds and european investment bonds, carbon taxation and financing for development objectives. as regards taxation of the financial sector, we start again from a basic and commonly accepted assumption: that the financial sector, although it has the main responsibility for the crisis, although it has created and continues to create, despite the crisis, surpluses, is taxed as it is almost universally exempt from value added tax. a second also commonly accepted assumption that comes simply from looking at the numbers, the facts, of how the volume of financial transactions has evolved and grown over the last decade, is its great and ever-expanding divergence from its core role of financing the real economy. these two assumptions are widely accepted by parliament, but also by the european commission through its recent communication on taxation of the financial sector. so we are dealing with a clear injustice which must be rectified, and we must send a strong message to the european citizens that we have indeed learned from the crisis, that we are seeking the fairest possible burden-sharing, and that we are determined to take all the necessary measures at the global and european level to restore the financial sector to its essential role of financing the real economy. there is a broad consensus that the most appropriate tax instrument to achieve these objectives is the financial transaction tax. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the tax is not imposed on the value of goods and services, and that the tax is not imposed on the value of goods and services. as we all agreed in paragraph 13, 'a financial transaction tax can help to curb the most harmful practices in trade, such as short-term and high-frequency trading, and to curb speculation'. it is obvious that the first choice for all of us is to introduce this tax on a global scale. but it is equally obvious that, despite initial ambitious statements, the chances of a global agreement are being reduced rather than increased. the question is what are we in europe doing, hiding behind the lack of global agreement? is this enough and, more importantly, is it convincing for our citizens who are bearing the brunt of the crisis? even if it is not easy to proceed directly to the introduction of a financial transaction tax at european level, because it is not easy to reach a unanimous decision in the council, the european parliament, as the only european institution directly the rapporteur. - the mr president, at a time when the union is considering the future of the cap, it is even more essential to ensure that there is coherence between agricultural policy and external trade policy. the european agricultural sector is being asked to contribute increasingly to the production of public goods through strict standards of safety and quality, environmental protection and animal welfare. it is therefore logical that imports of agricultural products should provide the same guarantees. the union has long been, and to some extent still is, on the defensive in the wto negotiations on agriculture. however, some misconceptions which do not take account of the radical revision of the cap should be mentioned. the union has drastically reduced trade-distorting aid, in contrast to other major partners. it has also unilaterally drastically reduced export refunds, while competing trading partners continue to make extensive use of other forms of export incentives. the union is also the world's largest importer of commercial products from developing countries. the union has already made an extremely generous offer in the agricultural negotiations, which has not, however, been matched by an equivalent level of ambition by other developed and advanced developing countries. at the same time, the commission is conducting bilateral and interregional negotiations with a large number of trading partners. the impact on the european agricultural sector of all the individual agricultural concessions, alongside the pending agricultural negotiations, is of particular concern to us. in this context, commissioner, we call on the commission to preserve the multifunctional nature of the union's agriculture and the european model of agri-food products, which is a strategic component of the european economy. we would point out that concessions to agriculture can in no way be the currency of exchange for increased access to the markets for industrial products and services. in any event, we stress the need for an impact assessment prior to the opening of negotiations and in any event before the exchange of offers. the commission is also called upon to promote the competitive interests of the european agricultural sector and the competitive advantage of the union's high quality agri-food products. in particular, to ensure that our partners protect geographical indications more effectively both in the framework of bilateral trade agreements and in the framework of the acp-eu and wto agreements. in conclusion, agriculture is not just an economic activity. it supplies public goods of major importance to society as a whole whose supply cannot be secured through markets. the main challenge therefore lies in the effective combination of commercial and non-commercial parameters. the economic geography of the cap therefore, ladies and gentlemen, makes it imperative to ensure greater coherence between the agricultural policy and the union's external trade policy, between the internal aspects of the common agricultural policy and the external aspects of the agricultural policy, or, if you like, between what we call in foro interno and in foro externo, that is to say, the union's presence on the world trade scene in both its bilateral and multilateral aspects.

in writing. i voted in favour of the report on the guidelines for the 2012 budget. the report's general principles and objectives are moving in the right direction, stressing that the next eu budgets should focus on policies to boost employment and national economies (the total eu budget for implementing the flagship initiatives by 2020 is estimated at €1.8 trillion). however, it is important to stress at all times that the achievement of the objectives set by the europe 2020 strategy is also a necessary condition for member states to adhere to them. unfortunately, as the european commission has found, national plans to date do not deliver on key priorities of the strategy, such as increasing employment to 75% by 2020 from 69% today.
in writing. i voted against the single european act because it is inspired by the bolkestein directive which establishes the principle of the country of origin and thus allows for different treatment between workers in terms of wages, conditions, working time, social protection, etc. the same approach applies to workers from 'third countries' outside the european union. the commission is proposing to introduce a new system of equal treatment for european and non-european workers, thus increasing the competition between them and between foreign workers, depending on whether they are posted, seasonal workers, students or residents. these differences only enhance exploitation and precariousness. despite the mobilization of the european trade unions and the progressive forces in parliament for full equality of rights for all workers, the text reflects mainly a compromise between the right and the socialists. the future directive will not apply to posted workers or students, will allow discrimination on grounds such as language proficiency, and will deny family benefits to the families of seasonal workers. in addition, the call for ratification of the un convention on the protection of the rights of migrants and their families has been removed.

in writing. i voted against the report on migration flows because, despite the fact that there is a fairly correct and balanced analysis of the main causes that force people to leave their home, the report does not draw the corresponding conclusions and proposals. on the one hand, it insists on a conception that divides people into legal and illegal and on the instrumental conception of 'useful' and non-immigrant, thus linking their rights according to the various 'quotas' of the union and the member states. on the other hand, the report links the phenomenon of migration with security issues, creates confusion and identification between migrants and various criminal or 'terrorist' activities and thus reinforces the practices and ideologies that criminalise them. in this context, the report, while further strengthening the union's 'paternalistic' role, goes so far as to propose linking the pillar of eu development aid to third countries with the pillar of 'security', thus completely changing the nature and purpose of this aid.

member of the commission. − i would like to thank the honourable member for his question because it gives me the opportunity to inform the house about shark finning. finning has been banned since 2003, via a council regulation, on eu vessels fishing anywhere in the world and on all vessels fishing in eu waters. in general there is a ban on shark finning. however, the current regulation allows – and this is the problem we face – under certain conditions, on-board processing involving the removal of fins on board vessels, while making obligatory the retention of all shark carcasses on board. this is why we have faced the problem of shark finning in recent years. we presented a plan of action in february 2009 and have since taken a number of measures. we are also actively working with regional organisations to put effective management regimes in place for the most vulnerable shark species and to ensure their sustainable exploitation. so the problem we are facing with a view to addressing this situation is the need for a public consultation, and we have now already had a public consultation for some months. the consultation document presented three of the main options that are currently being discussed by experts worldwide to improve controls and to ensure full compliance. many stakeholders, such as the fishing industry, scientists, managers and ngos, as well as the general public, have sent us their comments. i would like to assure you that i take the issue of protecting sharks very seriously. i have therefore asked my services to thoroughly study all the contributions received. we will then prepare an impact assessment which, as you know, is required to modify the regulation. it is my intention to have a legislative proposal adopted as soon as practically possible. i would like to inform you that i have made this issue a priority in order not to lose any more time. i would also like to say that the commission has taken a lot of measures to ensure the sustainable management and protection of sharks in general, beyond shark finning. we presented a plan of action and have since taken a number of measures. we have prohibited fishing for porbeagle, basking shark and white shark in eu waters. we have banned gill nets below 200 metres to protect deepwater sharks. last year – and i would like to underline this – we proposed a sustainable and science-based quota for various sharks. we had a very rough time negotiating this in the council. it was not an easy task, but in the end we were successful and we have a sustainable proposal for this year and, i hope, for next year.
member of the commission. − i agree with the members of parliament that although there is a ban, we cannot be happy with this situation. i agree with you and we know the reality and how it works. we member of the commission. − on the 3% r&d intensity target the state of innovation urgency in europe calls for the support of smart growth and a commitment to tackle societal challenges. the innovation union scoreboard shows that the eu is losing ground to the united states and japan, while brazil and china are closing the gap with the eu. the 3% r&d intensity target has a crucial contribution to make in meeting this challenge. the european council invited member states to set ambitious and realistic national targets, taking into account the initial level of r&d investment and the key structural characteristics of their economies. last year member states and the commission engaged in bilateral dialogues. nearly all of the member states have now set national r&d intensity targets, to be finalised in their national reform programmes by the end of april 2011. on 12 january this year, the commission adopted the communication on the annual growth survey. it comprises the list of national r&d targets, which are generally both ambitious and realistic and marks the start of a new cycle of coordination in this field. an assessment of the national research and innovation policies and achievements will be performed, aiming at identifying the main bottlenecks impeding growth and recovery in a post-crisis scenario where the financial constraints are still effective. an excellent research base is vital if the 3% r&d intensity target is to be achieved and if europe is to become more innovative. europe will need at least one million more research jobs if the r&d intensity target of 3% is to be reached by 2020. the number of new researchers required is significantly higher as many researchers will retire over the period. research excellence by universities and also, of course, by industry will benefit the wider society. progress is related to the high quality of higher education institutions. the innovation union scoreboard uses internationally recognised indicators to benchmark the performance of europe against that of our competitors. three of these indicators are: new doctoral graduates per 1 000 population aged 25 to 34, quantitative, international scientific co-publications per million population and scientific publications among the top 10% most cited publications worldwide as a percentage of total scientific publications of the country, both qualitative. the united states has increased its lead in international co-publications and is now 37% above the eu level. pending the results in june of a feasibility study, the commission will support an independent multidimensional international ranking to benchmark the performance of higher education institutions. this study will cover performances, not only in the field of research, but also in other important fields such as innovation, education, regional engagement and internationalisation. the multidimensional character of this concept will allow students, policy makers and the universities themselves to select the dimensions and underlying indicators of interest to them and make their own personalised ranking tailored to their needs. stakeholders are actively involved in all stages of this feasibility project.

certain beneficiaries, in particular the requirement for beneficiaries to allocate personnel and indirect costs to projects while deducting various items considered ineligible for eu co-financing. in member of the commission. − the new waste framework directive has set up a five-step hierarchy for waste management. waste prevention is regarded as the most desirable option, followed by preparing waste for re-use, recycling and other ways of recovery, including energy recovery, with disposal such as landfill as the last resort. deviations from the hierarchy for specific waste streams are possible. however, member states departing from the hierarchy would need to provide a sound justification. therefore, waste disposal in landfills that lie at the bottom of the waste hierarchy must be considered by the member states as the least favourable waste management option. high purity of waste materials, such as paper and glass, is a prerequisite for the use of waste as a secondary raw material by manufacturing industries. that is why separate collection of recyclable waste streams at source is usually the most favourable method of waste collection. under the waste framework directive, member states are obliged to introduce by 2015 separate collections for paper, metal, plastic and glass. again there is certain flexibility for member states to adapt their waste collection systems to the specific national circumstances, notably in cases where highly efficient and advanced sorting technologies are available. in the absence of such technologies, however, separate collection at source is the cheapest and the easiest method to obtain high quality secondary raw materials from waste. greece faces serious problems with illegal landfill disposal and was condemned, as you know, by the court in 2005 due to the huge number of illegal landfills that had been operating in its territory. this issue has not been resolved yet. nevertheless, in december 2010, the greek authorities provided an action plan according to which all the legal landfills will be closed by the end of june this year. the commission welcomes this plan, including the construction of new landfill sites, under the condition that this is unavoidable as a last resort option to maintain the waste disposal network that meets mandatory sanitary standards in line with european legal requirements. the construction of landfills complying with the standards of the eu landfill directive is already progress compared to the practice of illegal dumping of waste. the commission urges the greek authorities to complete their planning and the construction of the landfill sites – programmes that benefit already from eu funds. however, greece must steadily go beyond these measures and move away from landfill as a predominant waste management option towards a modern waste management policy based on waste recovery and recycling. according to the latest eurostat statistics, in greece around 82% of municipal waste is land-filled whereas the average in the european union is 38%. additionally, the performance of the recycling sector in greece is very low and only 17% of municipal waste is recycled. the implementation of the waste directive is a top priority both for the commission and for me personally. we will monitor the national waste policies through the assessment of the member states’ waste management plans. we are waiting for an updated waste management plan from greece. in addition, we are carefully monitoring the implementation of the greek action plan and the process of closing all the illegal landfills, including the plan for the eu-funded projects. we will also monitor the use of eu funding to ensure that the projects to be financed are consistent with the objectives and requirements defined in our waste legislation. in the case of greece, it is essential to reduce landfill and to increase recycling rates through separate collection and recyclable materials. proper waste management should be seen as an opportunity as it can create business and jobs across the country. it is also essential to achieve the new resource sufficiency objectives through the application of best practices. finally, tomorrow i am flying to greece, where i will be on a two-day full visit and we will, of course, discuss all these questions in detail there.

rules of procedure of the european parliament relating to the statute for european political parties and their financing by the european parliament. although there is a similar regulation, so far parties at european level that contribute to the formation of european political awareness and to the expression of the will of the citizens of europe. the european parliament has been a key player in the process of european integration, and it is the european parliament that has been the driving force behind the european union's development. that is why, after accepting the report of the secretary-general on the financing of political parties and his recommendation on the establishment of a regime, as well as the recommendation of the european parliament in the previous report of 2003 on the need for such a regime - but the treaty of lisbon had not yet been adopted at that time - and finally the decision of the bureau of 10 january, the committee on constitutional affairs, after serious consultation with all political parties, presidents and secretaries at european level, as well as distinguished professors of economics and constitutional law, and after consultation with the international transparency and the court of auditors of the european union, which approved this report, demands that the european commission actually submit a proposal for a european political party regime. the report also states that the system will have to meet certain criteria, namely that it must have national parties as members in at least seven countries, or regional parties, provided that the regional authorities in those countries have legislative powers. at the same time, there will be a distinction between the recognition of european political parties and their funding. in order to be funded, they must have elected at least one member of the european parliament. of course, parties will be able to register individuals, ordinary citizens, as members, in addition to having parties as members. the proposal covers not only european political parties but also their foundations. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the protection of the european communities' financial interests is a very important one, and it is a very important one. the european parliament has discussed the matter at length and has come to this proposal with only minor variations, which are, of course, reflected in the amendments. in essence, it concluded that it was a question of strengthening democracy, of increasing the presence of citizens in the european institutions by creating such a system, and, of course, as regards financing, it was stipulated that 10% should come from own resources and that there was a possibility for donors to increase the amount of eur 12 000 to eur 25 000, which was the case until now. i thank you, mr president, and i ask the house, of course, to vote in favour of this report.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think that the european union is being tested, in addition to the economic crisis, by a crisis of democracy and a crisis of legitimacy. the policies implemented anger and frustrate citizens, the decision-making processes alienate them from participation, as the recent european elections have shown. the european parliament has always been a party of the people, and it is the european parliament that has always been the party of the people. the rules of political and legal recognition and the necessary funding must therefore facilitate their action, allow them to develop their policies and their alternatives freely - that is the essence of democracy - and be free from external constraints, political or economic. i therefore have reservations about certain points in the report, in so far as they could be used as restrictions on the free and independent organisation and action of political parties. the functioning, action and organisation of parties must be a matter of their own choice and not under the pretext of a dominant political association.

the next item is the report by mr vital moreira, on behalf of the committee on international trade, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the introduction of autonomous emergency trade preferences for pakistan (com (2010) 0552 - c7-0322/2010 - 2010/0289 (cod)) (a7-0069/2011)
mr president, i am obviously in favour of the european union providing humanitarian aid to the extent possible. i understand the commission's reasoning for providing aid in the form of unilateral trade concessions to pakistan. however, i cannot agree with the commission's proposals, which call for the burden to be borne mainly by two industrial sectors in the union, namely the textile industry and bioethanol. i would point out that the european textile industry has been under severe pressure in recent years as a result of the liberalization of trade within the world trade organization. ladies and gentlemen, i have been a member of parliament for four terms in a region whose naoussa region now has one of the highest unemployment rates in europe, and this is due to the effects of globalisation on the textile industry. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. it is not lost on us that these are two industries in which pakistan is particularly competitive. furthermore, these concessions are not linked to a conditionality clause as would be the case if pakistan were granted gsp+ (general system of preferences+) status. finally, i would like to ask whether these concessions will benefit the flood victims themselves in pakistan. let me doubt it! and to measure the good intentions here, i propose concessions on other industrial products. why specifically in textiles? we would be equally useful against the flood victims of pakistan. in any case, the duration and scope of the concessions should at least be limited and safeguard measures should be provided for as proposed in the epp group's amendments.
mr president, the achievement of an ambitious and mutually beneficial union-india agreement is rightly a central objective of the union's current external trade policy. the rapid conclusion of the negotiations requires intensified consultations in critical areas such as services, non-tariff barriers, public procurement and geographical indications. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's trade policy is not distorted by the introduction of new tariffs. as regards access to services, unfortunately, there is no clear commitment from the indian side at present. the union should firmly insist on its demand for enhanced protection of all geographical indications in such an important market as the indian market. india is also an ally of the union in the doha round multilateral negotiations on geographical indications. it is noted that the indian legal system is clear, in particular as regards the registration procedure for geographical indications and their co-existence with trade marks. finally, i should say that the union must show flexibility in response to the request of the indian side to provide protection for indian non-agricultural geographical indications in order to provide protection for european geographical indications.
the commission's proposal for a regulation on the protection of the financial interests of the european communities is a very good one. however, until such time as it is possible to conclude investment agreements at union level, the legal vacuum, the legal uncertainty as mr caspary said, must be avoided and the necessary legal certainty must be provided for european investors. i would point out that the legislation of the member states of the union, in conjunction with eu legislation, provides all the necessary guarantees for investors from third countries. conversely, ensuring a high level of protection for europeans investing in third countries requires that existing bilateral agreements concluded by individual member states of the union be maintained. the draft regulation, in my view, does not at all provide the necessary legal certainty. i would like to refer in particular to the points concerning: first, the discretion which the commission retains to withdraw authorisation to maintain existing agreements or to authorise the opening of negotiations to amend existing agreements or to conclude new agreements; second, the provision for a review of the legal framework within five years; and third, the extremely time-consuming procedures for concluding new agreements. the amendments adopted by the committee on international trade are, in my view, moving in the right direction. i repeat, the aim should be to maintain the existing ones and to simplify the procedure for concluding and implementing new bilateral agreements.
madam president, today's europe day reminds us of the objectives on which the european union must be based: the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. but the euro pact is moving in the fundamentally wrong direction, as it is exhausted in imposing traditional economic orthodoxy. the attempt to link the euro to permanent cuts in the welfare state and permanent pressures on wages and pensions in the long term threatens to erode not only political cohesion but also the european idea. the greens oppose all this to the pact for sustainable prosperity: complete fiscal convergence, a european budget that is genuinely interventionist and ambitious, taking into account the social and environmental dimensions everywhere. so we want to lay the foundations for moving in a different direction. but no one has the right to make decisive decisions without the citizens! the only solution is a meaningful dialogue and direct appeal to the people. the arrogance of those who have handled the european constitution in the past has prevented us from having the european referendum institutionalized. but we can find alternatives if we have the political will. we owe it to europe and its future!

the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. one of the most tangible outcomes of the cancun climate change negotiations was the agreement on a green climate fund, with an unprecedented funding of $100 billion. as the un transition commission prepares the final form of the fund with a view to receiving a final stamp of approval at the end of the year in durban, questions remain open regarding the design of this unique and extremely important tool. the fund should be a well-designed vehicle to provide effective financing for climate adaptation in the developing world. but both the latest criminal attacks on the eu emissions trading system (eu ets) and the evidence of a recent transparency international report on corruption in climate finance should concern us. the commission has already taken the necessary steps to ensure that the european parliament is able to express its views on the matter, and i hope that the council will be able to take the necessary steps to ensure that the european parliament is able to express its views on the matter.
the rapporteur. - the the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of forests against fire and other harmful substances is a very good one. forests are part of our identity. it's our recreation, it's our business. and yet forests are so different for each of us, for each region of europe. if you visit the mediterranean forests from northern europe, you will see many areas that we in the mediterranean would call forests as savannahs or parks, as they have no productive activities. or, conversely, someone from the mediterranean travelling to northern europe would find the forests of this region to be more man-made than natural, as they are very heavily used for production. these forests, which are so different for each of us individually in europe, for each of our regions, have a common threat: climate change. climate change is threatening europe's forests through increased fires, disease, cross-country transmission that threatens entire species, and other disasters from extreme weather. the impact varies from one geographical area to another, but it is transnational and requires europe's help in addressing it. we are discussing today and in two days' time we shall be voting on the report of parliament on the protection of forests. it is a report which has been drawn up by consensus, from the outset, in cooperation with members of parliament from all countries and political groups. when it was put to the committee for discussion, a process of 50 compromise amendments to further develop the report was followed by all the political groups and regions represented in europe. i am therefore confident that this report represents parliament's view on how we can help forests, help our societies to adapt to climate change. what are we asking for in this report? we ask the commission to follow up the white paper on adapting and protecting forests to climate change, we ask for a new regulation to replace the old one on forest fire prevention, we ask for a new regulation to replace the old one on forest information, and we ask for an increase in funding for forests under pillar 2 of our common agricultural policy. forests account for 42% of the countryside, yet they receive only 1% of the cap. we are calling for the possibility of financing public bodies, for sustainability criteria for the forest biomass we use for energy and finally for active, sustainable forest management adapted to climate change.

in writing. frontex, in view of the increased migratory flows, is called upon to play an active role in the protection of europe's borders. according to frontex, 95% of illegal migrants entering europe enter through greece. the cost of deporting an illegal immigrant is €6,500 and, under dublin iii, the country of entry is responsible for deporting him. the countries on the eu's external borders are under all the migratory pressure and have become the 'migration warehouses' of the whole of europe. frontex must be supported financially and operationally to strengthen the protection of the eu's external borders and provide for a mechanism for distributing the total number of migrants across all european countries.

exclusion, reducing the proportion of early school-leavers to under 10%, and ensuring that at least 40% of the younger generation will have completed a tertiary degree by 2020. the commission helps joint employment report, which is based on the commission’s assessment of the member states’ draft national reform programmes, calls on them to improve the functioning of the labour market by integration of women into the labour market, ensuring that pension reforms include a more direct link between later retirement and increased pension entitlements, removing incentives for people to which is why it is difficult to talk about figures at the moment - the general economic context and framework in which the budget is discussed. the member states are making efforts to reduce their expenditure, and it is also necessary that at european level we can focus the financial resources available on real priorities, on european added value. i think that in this way, mr kelly, we can justify a substantial budget for the common agricultural policy by the contributions of this policy to european society, not only in terms of marketable agricultural production but also in terms of non-marketable production, which is not remunerated by the markets. both in the payments to farmers and in the second pillar components, or through investment, through support for the production of local public goods, these objectives are being met. the proposals on the multiannual framework - as i said in my introduction - will come in june, and only then, in the autumn, will the commission present the legislative proposals. the measures taken at commission level are quite consistent, since the broad guidelines of this policy were already set out in the communication which the commission presented last november. the commission will come forward with proposals for the multiannual budgetary framework at the end of june. and on this basis, on the basis of the communication containing the broad guidelines of the reform, in the autumn the commission will present the legislative package. at that time we will not be in total confusion at all, since we will already have the presentation of the multiannual budgetary framework. the changes to the common agricultural policy will therefore not only be qualitative, in order to better target our objectives, but they will also be aimed at the distribution of payments between member states, within member states themselves or between the different categories of holdings in order to use the available resources more effectively in accordance with the objectives set. this rebalancing of payments not only serves to ensure greater fairness but also to better mobilise the different structures of agricultural production to meet the new objectives that are being set, since historical references to payments that were based on subsidies received previously are no longer justified in this context in which fairly clear objectives are now being set for the future common agricultural policy. mr niculescu, how can we ensure a good balance between the production of market goods, food goods and environmental goods? not by trying to put even more on the farmers, but by trying to use part of the budget as an incentive to produce through agricultural practices which are environmentally friendly, but which do not necessarily involve too great an increase in production costs. so, thanks to this incentive, and without greatly affecting the level of agricultural production, european farmers will also be able to produce public goods. but for this, it is clear that this production of public goods will be directly proportional to the level of budget that can be ensured to cover the costs with this type of agricultural practice. in this way, the common agricultural policy will be able to integrate, in the objectives proposed with this reform, economic aspects, environmental aspects, aspects linked to climate change and aspects linked to the balances of territories in rural areas.

member of the commission. - mr president, on a practical level, this can be ensured by encouraging farmers to adopt agricultural practices which not only respect the environment, soil quality, water and biodiversity, but which also enable farmers to reduce carbon emissions and better fix carbon in the soil. the second pillar of the common agricultural policy, in particular, is intended to encourage farmers to direct their investments towards reducing carbon emissions, including through measures relating to investment to enable farmers to modernise. for example, the level of public co-financing will not be the same for a tractor with high or normal carbon emissions as for a tractor and agricultural equipment with low carbon emissions. so we will use public funding to encourage farmers to care about this issue. secondly, it is envisaged to create an instrument that will contribute to a knowledge agriculture, i.e. that will make it possible to use the results of research, development, innovation - even research produced under the common research strategy - and to put all these results into practice. a network of good practice and innovation will be set up at european level, bringing together researchers, consultants, trainers, farmers, the agri-food industry, to shorten the chain of knowledge production to the practical application of this knowledge. in this way, the agricultural technologies and techniques that farmers will apply can also contribute not only to ensuring economic competitiveness but also to reducing the impact of agricultural activity on climate change.

member of the commission. - mr president, i thank corien wortmann-kool, sharon bowles and, now, antolín sánchez presedo for their three questions on a very important subject, the credibility of stress tests on banks. ladies and gentlemen, we are in a situation where the financial industry is slowly recovering - even though for some banks the crisis seems to have already ended - from this crisis, from an unprecedented violence. we are not done learning the lessons and there is important legislative work to be done. to assess this crisis and learn from it, we need a supervisory framework - we have had one since 1 january, thanks to you in particular. we need predictive tools, we need better governance in each of these institutions. we also need better capitalisation - we will come back to that. and then, we need to measure, take the temperature, take the pulse all the time. and that is why - as you have said, ladies and gentlemen - we need reliable measuring instruments at the moment. the stress test is a key measure, a key tool in this context and we have discussed it not only here but also often, and no later than in april, with the finance ministers in council. as you have mentioned, the stress test last year was clearly inadequate and the commission itself has said this on many occasions to the new supervisory authority, the eba, which is coordinating the test in cooperation with the national supervisors. so you are right to ask about the quality and, again, the credibility of the new tests in 2011, which started a few weeks ago in april, and i would like to answer your questions, give you our analysis on five points. first, the stress tests for 2011, as you requested, have been improved in real terms, particularly in six areas which i would like to tell you about by telegraph. 1. the the adverse macroeconomic scenario used simulates conditions that are much more stringent than the 2010 scenario. it adds, among other things, severe property shocks, as well as an explicit impact on the cost of financing. 2. the the consistency of the exercise was greatly improved by a strengthened upstream methodology and rigorous downstream contradictory validation. it's called peer review. 3. the in accordance with the principle of increased transparency, the publication of results in june will be enhanced and accompanied by a separate but detailed publication of bank balance sheets. this will also include publicity of sovereign debt holdings as well as capital structure. 4. the banks are also tested on the basis of a higher capital threshold, the core tier one. the fifth. the publication of the methodology in advance of the publication of the stress results improves the overall credibility of the exercise. 6. the finally, the coordination of national authorities in the implementation of the solutions, which will be imposed on banks that fail this test - the so-called backstops - is significantly strengthened and improved. this is the progress, the improvement which you were right to call your wishes and which has been made in one year compared with the previous one. secondly, ladies and gentlemen, we need much more clarity on sovereign debt exposures. many of you, particularly the liberal group, have asked me about the methodology used in this context, as mrs wortmann-kool did earlier. the eba's adverse scenario envisages a significant shock in the form of changes in the price of sovereign debt and the cost of its financing. but as you pointed out, this scenario does not extend to sovereign default. the impact of the shock as envisaged by eba would only have an impact on the sovereign bonds held in the banks' trading book. nevertheless, there is an explanation for this choice made this year. i would remind you that stress tests simulate extreme scenarios, but they must be plausible. today, and in the context of the recent establishment, with many euro area governance tools, of the new european financial stability mechanism and the european financial stability facility, we reasonably think and we think with the european banking authority that it is much more useful today to ensure full transparency of sovereign debt exposures as they appear in the banking and trading book. the advertising will be much more detailed than last year. third point. you also drew our attention to the need to implement more coherent stress test scenarios across the union. this is indeed essential for the credibility of the exercise. the authority is making considerable efforts to conduct a rigorous validation of the results of this year. this will ensure consistency between the methodologies applied by the banks and, i believe, appropriate convergence in the way macroeconomic scenarios are translated into the respective risk parameters. this approach does not prevent banks from reflecting certain specificities of their portfolio or a particular management model. another key element in the consistency of the exercise is the use of common definitions of the capital thresholds against which the participating banks will be assessed. the capital benchmark announced by eba is largely based on the current provisions of the capital adequacy directive, which already takes into account the different banking structures and management models that exist in europe. fourth point. you asked us about the differences in coverage of the banking sector within the union, as did sharon bowles and other speakers. the authority has endeavoured to develop a sufficiently representative sample, both at national and eu level, while maintaining a manageable fiscal year. the banks tested in the 2011 financial year represent, ladies and gentlemen, 65% of the european banking sector in terms of total assets. in each member state, the sample was drawn up to cover at least 50% of the total assets of the national banking sector. i come now to my fifth point, which mr sánchez presedo has mentioned, concerning the question of the corrective measures, the backstops, expected from banks which prove to be vulnerable or potentially undercapitalised. these banks will have to implement appropriate measures to address their weaknesses, in particular by turning to the private sector for financing directly from the markets or by selling assets. if, and only if, these measures prove insufficient, public support could be considered, provided of course that it complies with european state aid rules. my colleague joaquín almunia and his whole team are working upstream with the member states on this particular issue. if public support is needed, the beneficiary banks should, in accordance with the december 2010 communication on the implementation of state aid rules for banks, submit to the commission a problem-based restructuring plan, in particular to strengthen and restore their long-term viability. finally, you have legitimately called for a strategy for recapitalising and restructuring failing banks, as proposed by elisa ferreira in her report on crisis management. as you know, ladies and gentlemen, we are working on a legislative framework for crisis management, banking resolution, we have had the opportunity to speak about this on several occasions. my aim is to give supervisors and the future resolution committee for these transnational institutions a toolbox to take preventive measures, to prevent risks that have been diagnosed early enough from turning into crises and crises from turning into catastrophes. so, to ensure and finance if necessary early intervention, that the banks pay for the banks, that is what we have called an orderly resolution, and i intend to put this proposal before both the council of ministers and you before the end of this summer. these are the most precise technical answers i could give to the three extremely pertinent questions that were asked at the beginning of this meeting.
the s&d group is calling for a new approach to the problem of the environment. commissioner, if we have learned anything in europe from the recent financial crisis, it is that fully ensuring the adequate capital adequacy of our credit institutions and effective supervision of the level of risk they take on are key elements of overall governance, not only financial but also economic. the european economy's return to growth in a lasting and consistent way also requires the restoration of confidence in the functioning of the banking sector and the general restoration of the smooth functioning of the financial system in terms of transparency, but also in terms of returning to its basic role as a lever for financing the real economy. as has been demonstrated in practice, and as several speakers have pointed out, last year's stress tests failed to achieve their objective, namely to demonstrate which banks have the required credibility vis-à-vis consumers, their creditors and national regulators. this year, we are in a different situation. the stress tests will be initiated by the new supervisory authority, the european banking authority, and we must by all means avoid last year's failure. a key prerequisite for this is the imposition of common criteria for assessing the resilience of banks, uniform in their interpretation and application, but broad enough to cover the different risks of each national market. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the financial interests of the european communities against counterfeiting is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr pimenta, for his report, which has been very helpful in this respect.

president-in-office of the council. − mr president, i fully understand the significant interest in this parliament in the actions being undertaken within the union and beyond to tackle the challenges which some member states are facing in relation to their public finances. the global financial crisis has had a significant impact on both revenues and expenditure in all our countries, even if the extent and nature of that impact is not the same in all cases and the capacity of individual member states to handle the consequences is also very different. the first thing i would like to stress is that it is the member states themselves which are, first and foremost, responsible for ensuring that their public finances are sustainable and on a sound footing. similarly it is for each one of them to ensure that their economies are competitive, flexible and resilient. of course, that does not mean that public finances and economic performance are not also a matter of collective interest. we are part of a union, and our economies are interlinked in a number of ways: through the single market and in many cases through the sharing of the common currency and the deeper economic integration which that implies. more generally, we all have a commitment of solidarity towards each other, based on a desire to protect and promote the wider european interest. what that means is that we all want to see a stable and strong economy across the eu as a whole and, within it, of the euro area in particular. where necessary this has to involve taking steps to ensure the stability of individual member states. we have a number of tools at our disposal to do this. we have the coordination mechanism that seeks to ensure that appropriate economic and budgetary policies are pursued by each and every member state. these are being updated and reinforced, and i am pleased that negotiations between the council and parliament are advancing well. we also have access to the european financial stabilisation mechanism, which can offer support at eu level to any member state, whether inside or outside the euro zone. in addition, and for the euro zone countries specifically, further instruments have been set up and are continuing to be developed. greece has received a package of coordinated bilateral loans from member states as well as a loan from the imf. ireland has received a package consisting of bilateral loans, a loan from the european financial stability facility (efsm) and also a loan from the imf. the support package for portugal, which will also draw on both european and imf support, is also being prepared. ministers of the euro zone member states are also finalising the technical details of the european stability mechanism, which is due to take effect with the programme for the first quarter at its meeting on 17 may, next tuesday. i cannot say much in advance about that discussion, but the overall assessment is likely to be that ireland’s performance is in line with expectations. however, some specific challenges remain. ireland will, in particular, need to stick to the powerful fiscal adjustment as well as ensure that its financial sector is on a stable footing for the future. second, greece. greece has come a long way since the very difficult situation last year, and its efforts should be commended. it has been faced with a daunting challenge and has demonstrated unwavering commitment and clarity of purpose. the adjustment programme is broadly on track. the latest implementation report, drafted jointly by the commission, the imf and the ecb in march, concluded that the programme has made further progress towards its objectives. some of the reforms needed to deliver the programme’s medium-term objectives are being put in place. the report also identifies further areas where reforms are required in order to build the critical mass necessary to ensure fiscal sustainability and economic recovery. the commission, the ecb and the imf continue to monitor progress on the implementation of the adjustment programme closely. the next review is scheduled for this month. the member states participating in the bilateral portuguese parliament had previously rejected the new fiscal conciliation package proposed by the government. negotiations between the troika and the portuguese authorities have now been finalised, and the memorandum of understanding on the policy conditions attached to the financial assistance is being agreed. the financial envelope will be around eur 78 billion covering a three-year period. in line with recommendations by the ecofin ministers at the informal ecofin in budapest in april, the programme covers reform in a number of areas, including public finance, labour and product markets and the financial sector. we consider that such measures are essential for growth potential and increased economic stability. endorsement of the final financial package is also expected at next week’s ecofin council. this is only a brief overview of the measures being taken to address the impact of the global financial crisis on the eu and on three member states in particular. as i said at the committed to doing its part to assist in ensuring that all necessary measures are in place in order to address the current problems. we consider that this is essential if we are to boost europe’s competitiveness in the longer term and, in so doing, deliver the strong role which europe as a whole needs.
