madam president, studies show that the phenomenon of the working poor is expanding due to the uncontrolled spread of new forms of informal employment, such as rotating and part-time work, fixed-term contracts, pseudo-employment, subcontracting, thus undermining the objective of the european strategy "europe 2020" to combat poverty. how and under what conditions do you think the new flexible forms of employment can be combined with the fight against poverty in order to ensure in practice both increased competitiveness and a socially positive overall result?
member of the commission. − the issue of the working poor is indeed a major and increasing problem. in the aftermath of the economic crisis – the great recession – we observe with great concern the increasing number of working poor. it is obvious that structural unemployment has been a key factor in increasing poverty. that is why we concentrated on fighting structural unemployment. i think there is an overlap here and the content of our agenda is key to this issue: investment in skills and focusing on how this could be reinforced by vocational training through lifelong learning in order to maintain the competitiveness of the labour force. in fact, the dublin foundation, eurofound, recently proved in a quantitative study that there is a so-called hollowing-out phenomenon in the labour market, which means that the second and the third quintiles have shrunk in terms of earnings, while the number of jobs in the lowest and the highest two have increased. it is the second and third which are in the greatest difficulties. we therefore observe a major problem in terms of the integrity of the labour market. this is also connected with the problem of segmentation, which we tried to address in the agenda for new skills and jobs. the answer is clearly partly legislative: to ensure that contracts offering earlier protection become more widespread; that young people get into permanent jobs more quickly after leaving school; and that in all member states there are more opportunities to invest in skills at all levels and thereby help employees preserve their competitiveness in the intensely competitive environment.

in writing. i think the council is making the same mistake again. it views the eu budget through a purely accounting approach as a budget of net expenditure. however, in the midst of the economic and social crisis that is plaguing europe and forcing member states to implement harsh austerity policies, we must defend the importance of the eu budget in boosting investment. it must be understood that the eu budget, which represents just 1.01% of eu gni, funds actions that either cannot be financed by the member states or that are financed at european rather than national level, which yields multiple benefits, mainly financial. that is its added value. it enhances the efficiency of national funding and leads to a reduction in overall expenditure by creating economies of scale through the concentration and coordination of resources and services. a typical example is the customs union, where 1 euro spent at eu level equals 4 euro savings for the member states. we must now, more than ever, call for support for areas that promote economic growth, such as cohesion policy, research and innovation, among others, thus strengthening efforts to save national resources and fiscal consolidation.
in writing. the proposal for a regulation on energy market integrity and transparency, which i supported, is a first step towards creating a european framework to integrate national energy markets into a single european market. the proposal concerns wholesale energy markets and aims to regulate deficiencies in wholesale energy markets, such as the suspension of energy production capacity. the european energy framework is of particular importance and will be of particular concern to greece, particularly in view of the discussions on the country's energy policy and the full exploitation of alternative energy sources (such as solar) offered by new technologies.
in writing. the report aims to increase the eu's accountability to its citizens at a particularly critical time. access to documents and information is one way - and certainly not the only way - to ensure citizens' participation in the democratic process and to enhance the transparency of eu policies and actions, as set out in articles 9 to 11 of the treaty. in any event, whilst full access is granted to legislative documents, exceptions are found to non-legislative documents, which should be kept to a minimum and justified only by strict criteria (e.g. disproportionate damage to the public interest). the report, which i voted for, included this aspect.
in writing. in the motion for a resolution on the state of play of the negotiations on the doha development agenda, i voted against. the current rules of world trade, imposed by the wto, serve the interests of already rich countries and large business groups while widening the gap between them and poorer countries. the failure to implement this agenda is therefore mainly due to the very nature of the wto. unfortunately, instead of ensuring the conditions for global sustainable development, free trade at all costs leads to increased social inequalities, the abuse of natural resources and the increase in environmental pollution. developing countries continue to view world trade from a disadvantageous position compared to the big players, who set the rules, one of which is the eu. finally, this motion for a resolution does not promote an alternative system of fair trade.
in writing. smart legislation is about implementing legislation in the eu quickly, while minimising administrative costs and red tape. however, it is recalled that the programme's target of reducing this administrative burden by 25% by 2012 is very difficult to achieve. further simplification and rapid ex-post evaluation of the procedures for transposing directives to member states is therefore necessary. the community institutions and the member states have a major role to play in this simplification of procedures. although the procedures are quite technical and administrative, the result of administrative obstacles is that the functioning of the eu on the one hand and the citizens on the other hand are faced with considerable difficulties. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full.
in writing. the phenomenon of homelessness not only persists in the eu member states, but in some cases it is worsening and a new category of homeless people, the so-called 'new homeless', is emerging. the european platform to combat poverty and social exclusion, while ambitious, cannot tackle the whole problem on its own and it is therefore essential that the eu take immediate, new strategic action beyond the formulation of opinions and reports on the subject. the resolution responds to these needs by proposing a strengthened and more dynamic strategy to tackle the problem of homelessness at eu level by identifying methods and instruments which will provide the best possible continuation of the work started by the commission on homelessness. that is why i voted in favour of it.

member of the commission. − the proposal for building the civil protection system of europe in a more predictable manner in order to act when a country is overwhelmed by disaster either inside europe or outside europe requires countries to identify modules, civil protection modules, which they are willing to deploy in a disaster outside of their borders. as of today, we have 124 such modules registered at european level, plus eight coordination modules, and the proposal means that we will be able predictably to match the needs of a country in a disaster, whether this be floods, forest fires or summer or winter storms or an earthquake, and then bring help from those pre-identified and pre-committed modules to the affected population. we already have examples of how this can be achieved. the proposal will take one step forward by having member states commit these modules to be available, provided they are not needed at home, for immediate deployment inside the european union or at the request of a third country outside of the european union. that brings the capacity of the european union together, to respond to disasters with a stronger force than we could provide for our citizens and the citizens of the world without this pre-commitment.

in writing. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'air traffic control' to cover all air traffic controllers. this will ensure non-discriminatory access to flights between the eu and mexico, but will also enhance flight safety levels.
in writing. europe, despite the economic crisis it is facing, is the most prosperous region on the planet. however, total expenditure on research, development and innovation (less than 2% of european gdp today) is significantly below the corresponding investments in other developed countries, such as the us and japan. the development prospects and, of course, the maintenance of the high standard of living are not therefore assured. on the contrary, circumstances call for a common and generous strategic framework for funding research and technology in the eu that will encourage entrepreneurship, innovation and development. they require strengthening the european research area and reorganising existing institutions and programmes, as well as bold policies such as financing, through the european investment bank, small and medium-sized enterprises that promote innovation. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one.
in writing. the kke opposes the report because it harmonises scientific research in the context of the anti-people eu 2020 strategy, which treats scientific research as a key pillar subordinate to capital. the report proposes financial support for the 'centres of excellence' and funding from the industrial sector. it encourages researchers to become entrepreneurs and seek funding so that scientific research can be exploited for the profit of capital. it called on the eu to set up research monitoring and financing teams at local and european level. in the context of the capitalist crisis, the research sector is an important part of the strategy of european union capital in developing its profitability and its competition with the large and emerging imperialist states. the eu staffs intend to invest large funds in research exclusively geared to the production of 'competitive products, technologies and services' (e.g. galileo satellite programme), through research mobility programmes (marie curie programme), centres of 'excellence' for researchers and institutes, private and public sector partnerships, grants to enterprises, so that research in universities and research centres can be more organically aligned with the strategy of capital. today, it is more timely and necessary than ever to free research from the laws of private property and monopoly profit.
in writing. in the context of regional development, the development and sound use of financial resources is crucial to eliminate economic, social and regional disparities, particularly for the least developed and disadvantaged regions. the inability to absorb funds is even more acute in the present circumstances, in the light of the economic crisis and the austerity policies chosen to deal with it. the report makes some correct assumptions about the importance of absorbing the structural funds and the cohesion fund from the regions of the union and identifies several of the problems in this process. i voted against because the 'public-private partnerships' method is presented as a solution to increase absorptivity and it is proposed that national legislation be amended to make it better and simpler to institute, with a view to further facilitating such partnerships. experience to date has shown that the public service compensation schemes, both at regional and local level, are designed to serve private profit rather than to maximise social benefit. the cost of implementing them is proven to be higher, their economic efficiency reduced and their quality low. finally, the benefits do not directly flow to local economies and societies but, on the contrary, create additional burdens and disruptions.
in writing. one of the most discussed political issues, not only in greece but also in the other member states, is the rate of absorption of community resources provided by the structural funds and the cohesion funds. low absorption rates are not always the result of weakness on the part of the member states but, in many cases, are due to problems inherent in the funds themselves (e.g. very specialised, unusable or less functional programmes which make absorption difficult). in any case, however, the absorption of resources is in proportion to the ability and adequacy of central and local authorities to draw up appropriate programmes and projects and to monitor the implementation of these programmes, avoiding possible irregularities. the report also identifies a common ground for all the member states and therefore for greece. recognises that the economic crisis makes it difficult for member states to participate in co-financed projects with the required national participation and proposes flexible practices to allow community resources to be released more quickly and invested more efficiently.
in writing. the report on 'a stronger european response to disasters', while stating as its main objective the strengthening and improvement of the european response to major disasters, contains several ambiguities on key issues of moral and social freedoms. first, the provision for triggering the 'solidarity clause' as formulated through the treaty of lisbon allows for the subjective attribution of terms such as terrorism and man-made disaster. the report also provides for the use of military means under civilian protection to deal with disasters without again diligently clarifying the nature of these disasters. finally, the prospect of the widespread use of opaque satellite monitoring systems such as galileo involves the risk of these systems being used for the purpose of monitoring the actions of social and political groups. i therefore voted against the report.
in writing. europe, like the rest of the planet, is experiencing increasingly extreme natural phenomena, natural and man-made disasters. the deadly fires, particularly in the mediterranean forests, which afflict greece almost every summer, are only one form of this. the european union has been the victim of a series of catastrophes that have cost european countries a total of over eur 210 billion over the last 20 years. this growing trend requires two main strategies. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the lisbon treaty meets these two conditions by establishing new legal bases for civil protection and humanitarian aid to ensure a rapid and effective response to disasters occurring in the eu and beyond. it is in everyone's interest that there should be a european civil protection mechanism, backed up with the appropriate resources and the necessary know-how to ensure its successful operation. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them.
in writing. the european parliament's report and the commission's communication are far from innocent. the eu legislative framework for the eu civil protection mechanism has already been extended to include actions to 'combat terrorism'. in this context, it proposes the establishment of a civil protection force on the basis of a 'all-hazards approach' with 'synergies between the various existing tools and instruments'. it proposes activating and implementing the 'solidarity clause' introduced by the lisbon treaty, which allows the eu to intervene in the internal political affairs and developments of a member state, including 'to counter threats to public order and security'. behind the loud calls to respond to forest fires or other environmental hazards or natural disasters, there are plans to use military means, as well as the use of existing monitoring systems such as the gmes and galileo satellite systems. the infrastructure and conditions are being created for close coordination and mutual support between military and civilian means so that an upgraded eu civil protection system can take on even more militarized characteristics and structure.
in writing. the european parliament's own-initiative report, which i voted in favour of, sets out proposals to make the eu the world's number one tourist destination. this is an objective of considerable interest to greece, particularly when the country is investing heavily in the tourist product in the hope that this will help to stem the negative growth rates of the economy. it is noted that tourism now accounts for more than 10% of european gdp, and an important point for greece in the report is the reference to the need to harmonise vat in order to avoid monopolies and to maintain them at levels that will make the tourist product of the member states competitive. although the report is not binding, it contains important proposals and strategic guidelines for boosting tourism in the eu, which member states can take advantage of.
in writing. i voted in favour of the fidanza report because europe must continue to take coordinated action to promote european tourism. european tourism is an important tool for promoting european culture and is an important source of income, particularly in some southern member states which do not have heavy industry.
in writing. despite the decline in road accidents, the eu still loses a city's worth of people (35000 victims) in fatal road accidents every year. road behaviour is certainly one reason for these losses. however, no one can deny the importance of well-built and modern road infrastructure in the effort to prevent road accidents. unfortunately, the economic crisis has led to many co-financed road projects being suspended or postponed due to the inability to pay the national contribution. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the road network is not affected by the current situation. the report by mr van miert, which i voted in favour of, recognises the challenges of the present and proposes flexible procedures to facilitate the absorption of resources. it also notes the need for quantitative targets for the member states and for the evaluation of national policies, by drawing up and publishing national road safety plans based on harmonised common guidelines.
in writing. i voted in favour of the koch report because road safety is a major european issue. it is worth noting that a coordinated approach to road safety, such as the reform of the road traffic code, better training and testing of would-be drivers and, in general, traffic lawsuits, are actions that have contributed to the percentage reduction in road accidents in europe. indicatively, there was a 37% decrease compared to the year 2000 and, as it seems, this decrease continues in 2011.
in writing. i voted in favour of the deva report on the financing of infrastructure for dam construction in developing countries because, considering that water is a vital resource for agriculture and for the livelihoods of the population of developing countries, the report's proposals are moving in the right direction. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the health of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster is a very good one.
in writing. the issue of food security and food self-sufficiency is of paramount importance to the eu. i therefore agree with the rapporteur's position on a more coordinated eu development policy in relation to global food security. the eu has a responsibility to respect the principle of 'doing no harm' to developing countries' food markets and to adopt a fair trade strategy. the question of fuels of agricultural origin is also very important, the production of which should in no case result in a reduction in the available agricultural production for food purposes.
in writing. the kke group in the european parliament voted against the relevant report on trade policy in the context of the europe 2020 strategy, which strengthens the aggressiveness of monopoly business groups in eu member states and third countries to plunder the people and boost the profitability of monopolies even in conditions of capitalist crisis. the people know that when the bourgeoisie speaks of "opening markets" - "free trade zones", they mean an attack on popular conquests, intensification of exploitation, increase in unemployment, poverty, imperialist interventions that will ensure the profits of the monopolies. it is in the interest of the peoples to reorganize and counterattack the workers' and people's movement, to build the people's alliance, to overthrow the anti-people policy, the power of the monopolies, to break away from the eu, with people's power and economy, where international trade will develop on the basis of mutual benefit for the peoples.

acting president of the council. - madam president! - what are you doing? i would like to thank mr. bowles and mr. berès very much for their questions. i think this is the first time we can attempt to make a 'preliminary' assessment of the functioning of the european semester and draw at least some of the conclusions that can be drawn at this stage as regards its practical application. i would like to emphasize that we can really only talk about the preliminary assessment, because the semester as such or the whole process has not been completed yet. this process, or at least its annual operation, is completed only when national parliaments adopt national budgets. this is the first time we can actually assess whether the whole procedure launched in january 2011 has had any positive effect: whether there is any new added value in national budgets compared to what was previously there, and whether what we all wanted has actually happened, namely greater synergy between the economic policies of the member states, greater concentration of resources in line with the main priorities of the european union. we do not know yet, the process is still ongoing, so it will be a matter of months before we can finally assess the effectiveness of the european semester. nevertheless, based on our first experiences, it seems to be a very legitimate process, desirable and taken very seriously by the member states, national parliaments and all the eu institutions involved in this process. i'd like to briefly recall how this process works. it starts at least as of this january when the european commission presents its annual growth analysis. on this basis, the ecofin council adopts some general guidelines for the member states in february. member states then have until april to prepare their national reform programmes plus stability and growth pacts or convergence programmes, depending on their stage of euro area membership. then there is the period for the european commission to prepare recommendations in agreement with the member states, responding to the comments made by the member states. then comes the very tense period in june, when the relevant sectoral councils, their groups, the preparatory bodies and the european council finally adopt these guidelines, which are - as in this case - finally confirmed by the ecofin council on 12 july. the timetable is very tight right now. we've already got some conclusions or some suggestions for the future on how to make this process better. however, i would like to point out that the european semester itself should be assessed in two aspects: the first aspect, namely the technical functioning of the european semester - what i have been talking about: how certain documents are adopted, how much time we have for this; the second element is the impact of the european semester on the macroeconomic dialogue in the european union and the involvement of the member states in this dialogue, on the impact of the macroeconomic situation, on public finances. this is the main element of the european semester, which is to link macroeconomic priorities with public finance opportunities and priorities. as regards the technical aspect, the first few months of the process of preparing the recommendations for the member states show that it is a very technical process, requiring a lot of work on the documents throughout the procedure. over 600 documents are prepared during the first six months. please note that most of these documents must then be translated into all national languages in due course. so it's a very complicated process logistically. we have a very tight schedule later in june, very short deadlines for all the relevant authorities to come forward and approve the relevant documents. there is little room for manoeuvre here, because the council's work schedule is so set up that there is really little we can change. so the question is, how can we make it even better? one of the suggestions that is coming up more and more clearly at the moment - and i hope that this will eventually be confirmed - is to start the whole process a little earlier. it is proposed that the european commission should present its annual report as early as december, giving the member states and the european union institutions a few weeks to prepare and to start this dialogue. so that by april we would be at a much later stage of discussion and coordination of member states' responses to the priorities identified in the commission's annual report and the preparation of documents on the reform agenda or the stability and growth pact would be more mature and better discussed. this will probably reduce the pressure that is particularly present at the end of may and in june: the pressure to ensure that all bodies are working efficiently and can accept all documents efficiently. i would like to point out how strong the determination of the member states was to make this process effective this year. as i said, there are a lot of documents, over 600. there are very short deadlines for opinion. therefore, member states have accepted certain derogations from the applicable rules. for a very large number of documents, the procedure was accepted even if not all the language versions were available. this is very difficult for many countries to accept, but they have expressed their willingness to do so, confirming their commitment to the process. they were only willing to work on the english or french version available at the time, in order to be able to speed up the work, to be able to conduct a practical dialogue and to adopt all the recommendations in due time. i would now like to turn to this second element, which is much more important to us, namely the assessment of the impact of the european semester process as a whole on the macroeconomic dialogue in the european union. we must remember that the european semester is only one of the elements that have emerged in the european union over the last few months as new instruments for closer economic cooperation between the member states and better implementation of the european union's priorities in this area. we have the european semester, the six-pack, which was adopted only recently, and the normal implementation of the stability and growth pact. all these elements form a certain whole and, at the same time, they bring much more transparency to the procedure, as well as much stronger dialogue between member states, much more transparency with regard to the actual economic situation in the member states. they also allow for greater pressure to be exerted on each other to keep the macroeconomic priorities in the right direction and to make everyone fully aware of the direction the union is taking and the challenges facing the member states. in my view, the sixth package has, in practice, introduced the involvement of national parliaments in the process of translating the eu's macroeconomic priorities for development into national policies through the strongest instrument available to a country, the national budget. national parliaments are informed at an early stage of the discussion about the priorities that a member state intends to communicate in its national reform programme, and about the budgetary approach that the member state will present, because they are informed about both documents submitted to the european commission. they then know the outcome of the european council's recommendations. they know what the european union recommends. the national parliaments then have the final say on the shape of the national budget, which means that they have a very good tool to control how national governments translate recommendations from eu priorities into national action. it is important that the european semester reinforces the direction of the european union's action, indicating one specific direction in which the member states should move. if the priority is to maintain or increase growth in some member states, to implement the europe 2020 agenda, then it is clearly marked and shown where the union should go, but at the same time it gives flexibility to individual member states, because we do not all start from the same place, but we all have to go in the same direction. this is very important. there is no one golden rule that everyone should follow, whether they need to or not. we have individual discussions about the member states, about their economic situation, we give them a clear message about where they should go, but we give them a fairly large margin of freedom in choosing the means to achieve that goal. the second important element that emerges is greater coordination and better targeting of the use of eu funds to achieve the priorities of the european union. national reform programmes, which set out how a country would like to spend at least a significant proportion of the funds it receives from the union, are integrated throughout the process. by coordinating this document with others related to the public financial management of the country concerned and with the eu priorities, by matching them all at the end of the road, we are sending a clear signal that the union has chosen these priorities, is ready to finance them and that we would also like - in the european union's view - that the country concerned subordinates its priority expenditure from the national budget to these objectives. then we will achieve the objective set for all the eu countries. the message is very clear now. in this respect, i think that the european semester has done very well, at least for the time being, in the council's view. how will this translate into the final national budgets? we do not know, because it depends on the decisions of the national parliaments. but the instruments are there, the opportunity is there and it must be seized. of course, it may turn out that our final evaluation after this year will still contain many questions and hints that we could have done something better. we must remember, however, that the european semester was introduced at a rather unfortunate time. we have a very big public debt crisis in the european union, we have some pretty significant problems with the banking sector. in fact, the union's economic situation is very dynamic. what we saw in april or may as priorities, as goals that are achievable in a given economic reality, in the reality of this spring, may prove to be either insufficient or impossible to achieve at this moment. it will therefore be easy in a few weeks to criticise the member states for not having done something despite the european semester. however, the dynamics of economic change in the european union and the development of the crisis are so great that it is really difficult at this moment to predict with a year's advance all the appropriate actions that should be taken. we must remember that all these instruments, the european semester, the six-pack, are designed to help us stabilise the macroeconomic situation in the european union and to give direction to our actions. but these are not the instruments that are supposed to free us from the problem of crisis in two or three weeks. these instruments were never designed in this way, so we cannot expect the application of the european semester to immediately improve the economic situation in the union. we believe that the european semester will significantly improve the macroeconomic dialogue in the union, which is its main objective. so far, the council's assessment is positive as regards the course of the proceedings. we are drawing more technical conclusions on how to streamline the process and give member states more scope to implement this process well, to participate fully and to have a better dialogue with the commission on these recommendations. there were questions about the european parliament's place in all this, whether it was a transparent process. the answer is yes, it is. all the documents are on the websites, they're public. anyone can participate in the process. the european parliament may also, in accordance with the new procedure, invite representatives of both the european council and the council to a debate, taking into account the macroeconomic situation. that's why i think things are going in the right direction.
member of the commission. − madam president, honourable members, thank you for giving me the opportunity to share with you our assessment of this first european semester and also our plans for the coming year. the first european semester has been an important step in strengthening our economic governance. it is part of an effort to rebuild confidence through a clear focus on building the foundations for employment and growth and through stronger policy design and implementation. we had clear expectations of what a european semester should mainly achieve in substance. firstly, we wanted to ensure a closer integration of the policy analysis and guidance across fiscal and macroeconomic policies but also of the policy formulation in member states. secondly, we wanted to ensure that the policy guidance given to member states has a stronger effect on implementation, through a better ex-ante timing of policy guidance and through clearer and more concrete country-specific recommendations. at the same time, the european semester was supposed to ensure that the eu-level dimension in terms of policy spillovers was taken into account from the start when formulating policies at national level. against these expectations the first european semester has been successful. we have made significant progress on these key elements. when it comes to assessing the effectiveness of ex-ante policy guidance in terms of the follow-up by member states, it is a bit too early to tell: we are, after all, only part way through the ‘national semester’. a measurable answer will therefore only be possible when member states’ budgets and structural reforms have been decided and we have assessed them. i count on this house to play a full part in making this assessment. we will then have to follow up on the implementation and examine what is the impact of the measures taken. there is a clear recognition on the part of most stakeholders that the policy guidance has become more integrated across policy areas and is more focused on countries’ central priorities. it has also been clearer and more concrete, which should facilitate implementation. with the joint presentation of their scps and nrps, member states have set out their views on how the key policy challenges should be addressed. the commission has assessed these policy plans and proposed integrated recommendations based on the broad economic and employment policy guidelines and on the stability and growth pact in terms of legal instruments. the annual growth survey has set the horizontal policy priorities for member states and ensured that national programmes take account of the eu dimension from the start. while i consider the european semester a clear success and an important step forward, there is naturally also scope for improvement. in 2012 the most important aspect is certainly going to be a stronger focus on the growth dimension. as president barroso outlined here on 12 october, bolstering growth, through full implementation of key reforms on the single market but also through new and innovative financing instruments such as project bonds, is a central dimension of putting europe on the course out of the crisis. you will certainly see eu-level action on growth and employment at the heart of the next annual growth survey. the commission has also decided to advance the presentation of the annual growth survey to late 2011. this should allow for a fuller debate from the outset. in our democratic societies, reform efforts can only be sustained if they have legitimacy, both in terms of being anchored in the democratic process and carried by the elected representatives of the european citizens as well as in terms of delivering what serves the common good. this means of course that this house, as well as national parliaments, will have to play an important role in the european semester. a strong link between the eu dimension and the national dimensions of key policy challenges can only be established if these perspectives are brought together through true ownership. this can only be achieved if parliaments have a strong role. i believe that the spring interparliamentary meeting which you organised in 2011 could, if repeated, become an important institutional way of better involving national parliaments to ensure legitimacy. and of course, the new economic governance legislation underlines the need for national parliaments – and other stakeholders – to be fully involved in the semester, and in the elaboration of the scps and nrps.
the s&d group is calling for a new approach to the problem of the environment. madam president, the european parliament, by a very large majority, had supported the european semester process from the outset, considering it a promising process aimed at bringing national budgets and structural change programmes in line in time, not with the objectives of the union in general, but in particular with the objectives of the development of the european economy. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. and, in the first implementation of the european semester, we had a rather limited text of substantial deviation of the member states from the development objectives under the europe 2020 strategy, but also failure to comply with certain recommendations of the commission per member state at the initiative of the council. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a step in the right direction, and it is a step which we are all very much in favour of. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the european semester is a good one, but it is not enough to say that the commission is not prepared to take action on the matter.
the commission is therefore proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work is a very good one. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. in my view, the implementation of the european semester is anti-social, anti-democratic and reactionary, as member states, under political pressure and threats from the commission, adjust their budgetary objectives and budgets. the implementation of the directive effectively removes any possibility for any member state, regardless of which government has voted, to implement an alternative development policy. on the contrary, whatever policy the people of each country have adopted, it must implement the neoliberal austerity policies of the european union. finally, whether in greece the unemployed person gets unemployment benefit, whether in ireland the poor and homeless person gets welfare benefits, whether in portugal the worker gets 300 euros, it will be decided by mr barroso or mr barroso or mr rennes. finally, a legitimization such as the european semester, which has no democratic legitimacy, which violates the treaties of the european union, which violates and bypasses the national parliaments, which bypasses the european parliament and, above all, which bypasses and violates and ignores the interests of the peoples, is a threat to democracy. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done on this subject. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. madam president, the european parliament, as the only directly elected institution of the european union, has the power to grant discharge in respect of the implementation of the general budget of the union. at the same time, the council's administration must be democratically accountable to european citizens for the use of union funds and comply with the relevant rules. however, the council administration has for a long time not accepted any invitation to meet the parliamentary committee responsible for the discharge procedure, which has not yet received answers to the questions it has asked. the european citizens, however, deserve better information on how their taxes are spent. i therefore believe that there should be no discharge and that if the last attempt at negotiation fails and if the council continues to take a different legal view of parliament's powers on the matter - given that the dialogue has so far reached a dead end and the legal backlog exposes all the institutions involved - we will now have only one option: referral to the court of justice of the european union to clarify this matter once and for all and to return to normal institutional functioning.
member of the commission. - mrs turunen, i can confirm that the european commission will honour the commitment it has made, and which president barroso has reiterated, to present all 12 key proposals before the end of this year. a number of these have already been presented. some of them are even very advanced. i was speaking earlier about the european patent. we have now put it forward for more than a year and i hope that it will perhaps be concluded, under the polish presidency, with a political agreement in the council. i would also add, to be completely objective, that in addition to the 12 key proposals we have committed ourselves to presenting before the end of this year, we are making progress on the other complementary proposals, mrs turunen. i take the example, under the control of neelie kroes, of the supplementary proposal on homelessness, which was a specific request by many members. neelie kroes didn't wait until next year. it has already put forward this proposal, which is one of the complementary proposals for the single market act. on the subject of the posting of workers, the aim of the new directive you mention will be to harmonize the implementation, under the authority of my colleague mr andor, of the directive on the protection of posted workers. at the same time, we want to remove unjustified obstacles to the free provision of services. we want to ensure that workers are properly protected and at the same time improve the functioning of the internal market. this proposal will contain provisions on administrative cooperation, on access to information for posted workers, on the prevention of abuses and circumvention - we know they exist - on control instruments, on sanctions and on legal remedies. the directive i have just mentioned for the implementation of the directive on the posting of workers would be aimed at its best practical application. we believe that the main purpose of this instrument will be to improve the information due to workers and businesses, administrative cooperation to make checks more effective and, once again, to prevent abuses which we know exist. we are not seeking to overturn the case law of the court of justice on this point, but we are going to make this directive to improve the implementation of the posting of workers.

in writing. as a lawyer and having experienced the burdens and delays in the administration of justice caused by the admission to greek courts of almost all civil and commercial disputes, i could not help but vote in favour of this report. the principle of private initiative, that is to say, the initiative of the parties, prevails in civil and commercial law, which makes these areas a prime area for the application of alternative dispute resolution methods, whereas the parties are seeking speed in the resolution of their cases in the interests of legal certainty, planning and competitiveness. the alternative dispute resolution, in the manner and for the disputes proposed, seeks to optimise the efficiency of the administration of justice, to achieve the harmonisation of the rules of alternative dispute resolution in the common market for the benefit of traders at the pan-european level and to bring about an acceleration of procedures. the commission's proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of their employer is a very important step in the process of harmonizing the laws of the member states. but the report is moving in the right direction.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report by which the european parliament refuses to grant the council discharge in respect of the implementation of the 2009 budget. the european parliament, the sole elected institution of the european union, has the power to scrutinise and, where it considers it appropriate, to grant discharge in respect of the implementation of the general budget of the european union, and therefore of all its individual institutions, with a view to providing european citizens with comprehensive and fully transparent information and ensuring democratic control and political evaluation of budgetary management. in the context of democratic accountability for the council's administrative budget, progress was made with the tabling of important documents by the council. the house also called on the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the european parliament's position on the draft directive is respected. the report rightly refuses to grant discharge until parliament has all the necessary documents and checks.
in writing. the report on mobility and inclusion of people with disabilities, which i voted in favour of, redefines the debate on the europe 2020 targets in the field of people with disabilities. i have, however, differed in paragraph 53 by voting in favour of the amendment calling on the member states to adopt the proposal for an anti-discrimination directive. member states continue to make very little effort to support this social group (a characteristic of many of them is that they have not signed or ratified the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities) while the economic crisis is leading several states, including greece, to make unacceptable cuts in public spending in this direction. the target of significantly increasing the labour market integration rate of people with disabilities (75% by 2020 from 30% today) is under threat, while the 1 in 4 proportion of people with disabilities currently living in poverty does not appear to be easing. it is clear that the eu and each individual member state need a new, more ambitious and obviously more generous strategy. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used in a way that is compatible with the common market.
in writing. the public procurement directive first came into force 40 years ago (directive 71/305/eec). the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it needs to be revised to meet both modern needs (simplified procedures to avoid red tape) and challenges (corruption and legal uncertainty). in the period of economic crisis in europe, bureaucracy is a potential impediment to the development of important development initiatives, while corruption and collusion are showing signs of intensifying. the reopening of the debate on public procurement is therefore timely and i support it for that reason.
in writing. the main argument of the report is that the best way to tackle unemployment is to promote labour mobility. according to this view, workers who lose their jobs because of the crisis and the austerity policies imposed across the eu, and more intensively in countries like greece, portugal and ireland, have no choice but to emigrate. although there are not enough jobs available at european level at the moment, the report fails to see that promoting labour mobility at all costs is contrary to regional and cohesion policy. the latter aims to support the endogenous economic and social development of europe's poorer regions, so that people can stay and find work there. the only solution to the problem of unemployment in europe is to overturn the policies which are being implemented, which are leading to middle-age working, flexible forms of work and are attacking wages and pensions. as this report fails to adequately address the real causes of unemployment and to propose radical and just solutions to reduce it, i voted against today's vote.
in writing. in times of economic crisis, labour mobility is particularly critical to economic growth and therefore the debate is timely. despite the fact that the eu is an area of free movement of citizens, only 2.3% of our fellow citizens say that they live in a member state other than their country of nationality. the reasons are many, such as language barriers, culture, emotional ties to the country, etc. in any case, however, member states at national, local and regional level have important responsibilities in facilitating the exercise of the right to labour mobility by removing any direct or indirect barriers. in particular, barriers linked to discrimination on grounds of nationality, denial of the right to family reunification, social security systems and other barriers may discourage or deter workers from seeking employment in another member state. the report aims to give concrete answers to these questions, it is moving in the right direction and that is why i voted in favour of it.
in writing. the mutual evaluation procedure of the member states on the functioning of the single market is by no means neutral in practice, since it is part of the european services directive and essentially takes its guidelines from it. in addition to its own unique shortcomings, such as the selection and composition of the working groups by the european commission alone, the mutual evaluation process is a key driver of the services directive, which refers to the failed eu 2020 strategy and the single market act. the implementation of this service directive, also known as the bolkestein directive, will not result in the increase in jobs and the growth of smes as advertised. through the further reduction of labour and social rights, resulting from the liberalisation of the services market across europe, it strengthens the dominance of large companies, while aggravating the consequences of the crisis for european workers. i therefore voted against the report.
in writing. the report on global economic governance is part of the prevailing conservative rationale of responding to the crisis by imposing stricter control and supervision of countries worldwide and closer coordination of their economic and fiscal policies. its aim is to institute global neoliberal economic policies at eu level, serving the interests of the 'leading economies' and international finance capital, imposing harsh austerity policies and demolishing the remaining social gains of the peoples. the commission is also proposing to strengthen the role of the imf in the eu and globally, and fully supports the anti-people and anti-social policies of the g20 which it calls for to be implemented immediately. the report is going in the wrong direction, because the policies it advocates will not help to recover from the crisis or to avoid another one, but will instead exacerbate the consequences of the international financial crisis, exacerbate social inequalities, poverty and unemployment worldwide, and lead, in short, to the 'global economic and social impoverishment' of peoples. i have voted against the report for all these reasons.
in writing. the evolution of the world economy, with the emergence of new major factors, calls for coordinated action at european and international level to combat the effects of globalisation. i voted in favour of the report because i think it is moving in the right direction, but there is a need for enhanced cooperation and far-reaching reforms that will promote growth and financial and macroeconomic stability in the economies. i share the rapporteur's view of the importance of correctly measuring imbalances with the help of a set of indicators which should cover both internal and external imbalances in order to achieve strong, sustainable and balanced growth. it is necessary to address coordination gaps in the financial regulations so that certain actors in the financial system are no longer given the opportunity to benefit from regulatory arbitrage.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report as it calls for greater attention to be paid to the situation of single mothers and encourages member states to adopt public policies, including policies in the areas of education, care, health, employment and social security. one in 20 women in europe is a single mother who needs support. this may limit the tragic reality of abortions. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the single mothers are not exposed to the threat of poverty and social exclusion. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the children of the elderly are not excluded from the family.
in writing. the single market and the divergence of national laws leave a wide margin of manoeuvre for organised crime. now, there's an even more complex variable. the economic crisis, which has given rise to other forms of organised crime exploiting the uncertainty and insecurity of citizens in particular. for example, greece, which has been hit hardest by the crisis, has recently seen a sharp increase in extortion (up to 50% in one year), smuggling (84.29%) and the circulation of counterfeit coins (56.99%). the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful organisms. the report i voted for is aware of the new challenges, but the commission should consider, in addition to the existing legislative initiatives, new, more effective legislative initiatives in this area.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report on the fight against organised crime in the european union because it is a fully legally based proposal, whereas it does indeed need to be considered in order to deal with this issue with particular care as it differs from terrorism. it is imperative that european states move aggressively to seize the proceeds of organised crime in order to condemn these practices and prevent their replication in the future. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to cover the whole of the european union, including the member states, and to extend it to cover the whole of the european union. the role of the foreign affairs committee is clear.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report. we must remember, however, that a successful policy is not only judged by its objectives, even if they have clear measurable criteria, but also by the means employed to achieve them. in fact, development aid cannot be effective if it does not take account of the specific economic, social and political characteristics of the country to which it is directed. it is not possible to deliver when it often substitutes for the domestic production of countries, virtually destroying any prospect of developing local productive forces, and when screening is often extremely inadequate, with the result that aid is lost between corrupt governments and organised crime. the stakes, of course, are not in sending aid unplanned, just so that the developed world can get along with its conscience, but in providing substantial and strategic support to our fellow men who need it to get back on their feet and move forward in today's globalized environment.

the next item is the report by regina bastos, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the agenda for new skills and jobs (a7-0320/2011 - 2011/2067 (ini))
member of the commission. − madam president, i would like to thank ms bastos for this report and all members of parliament for their proposals to strengthen the actions set out in the agenda for new skills and jobs. today we have to recognise that we face a challenge. it is a challenge for the european union as a whole, and for many other regions in the world: how best to support growth and the jobs which are so desperately needed in a climate of stringent fiscal consolidation. that is the challenge, and there is no easy answer to it. a lot depends on political leadership and decisions on the financial and economic crisis, but let us try to do what we can do, in the light of our roles. in order to step up the impact and visibility of the commission’s contribution to the europe 2020 goals and to meet the deadline – we are at about 75% of the target employment rate – we have undertaken to present a set of employment initiatives in early 2012. let me now inform you about those concrete actions. first, the commission will duly reopen the debate on flexicurity policy as a means of tackling labour market segmentation, so that everyone in europe, whatever their background or sector and wherever they live, can have a quality job. the conference on flexicurity on 14 november will provide an opportunity for all stakeholders to present their views on this key issue. secondly, in the present economic situation, there is unlikely to be net job creation in the union unless the member states step up their policy to stimulate labour demand. that is something we have to realise. there is nothing automatic about creating new jobs. the commission will therefore present principles for generating conditions that foster job creation for the benefit of all key players, including the public authorities and the social partners. thirdly, geographical and occupational mobility is a crucial way of tackling imbalances between sectors and regions where there is high unemployment and where there are labour shortages. the commission will therefore outline the way eures, our tool for mobility, can be modernised and turned into a powerful tool. we also intend to open a debate on how the union can face the situation of the mobile workforce, and particularly of migrants. we also need to see how employment policy might address the long-term challenges facing us so that we will be able to make the most of employment opportunities in the future. in particular, the restructuring of the economy and of businesses, as we discussed previously, and the transition to a low carbon economy, should be managed and anticipated better. lastly, the commission will bring forward proposals on developing a more strategic and integrated skills governance model. indeed, initiatives at national and eu level currently suffer from a lack of coordination and of mechanisms for exchanging information on the anticipation and analysis of skills. the most pressing challenge for our societies today is the high rate of unemployment among young people. that is the real problem. to tackle it, the member states committed themselves in june this year to implementing a comprehensive set of measures under the europe 2020 flagship initiative youth on the move. one particular concern is that 7.5 million young people aged between 15 and 24 are neither in employment, nor in education or in training. just imagine that. we are talking about 7.5 million young people. unless something is done they will become a generation of wasted talent. there is a wider and economic social cost such as tax revenue loss, the extra cost of health and medical services, the price to pay for crime and mainly social exclusion – we are talking about real social exclusion now. the young opportunities initiative announced by president barroso in his state of the union speech in this house will focus on many issues, including getting young people who have left school or training without any vocational qualification back into school or training and, secondly, providing opportunities for work experience to those who have a qualification but have not found work. the initiative will give the member states and all the actors involved the necessary support for delivering on the measures. as the report rightly points out, it is vital not to forget society’s most vulnerable and disadvantaged groups in this time of economic difficulty. here we have the european platform against poverty and social exclusion, and a commitment to lift out of poverty at least 20 million people by 2020. last week the first annual convention of the european platform against poverty took place in kraków, with very good results. let me finish by saying something about the eu’s future spending plans. on 6 october, the commission brought forward a proposal on cohesion policy legislation for 2014-2020, and on the role of the european social fund. we propose that after 2013 that fund should increase by at least 7.5% and thus account for at least 25% of cohesion spending, or at least eur 84 billion for the seven-year period up to 2020. the social fund will contribute to three of the five eu headline targets: employment, education and reducing poverty and social exclusion. our proposal for a regulation on the european social fund in the future involves allocating at least 25% of that in writing. the european parliament's report on the common taxation system for parent companies and subsidiaries of different member states is based on an existing council directive and essentially concerns its simple codification by way of a reformulation. i voted against because the report correctly points to the downward trend in the corporate tax rate in the eu and the absence of taxation or double non-taxation. the report itself also acknowledges that simple codification is not a solution to all the above problems. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption by the end of the year. the result is essentially to simply codify - and therefore continue - the dominant eu tax policy which is far from a socially just, acceptable and common european tax policy. a growth-oriented tax policy with a redistributive role capable of tackling the serious problem of tax competition, effective control and taxation of offshore companies and the dismantling of the notorious tax havens that also flourish in the eu.

acting president of the council. - mr president! - what are you doing? members of the european parliament! ladies and gentlemen! one of the greatest challenges facing modern medicine and public health is the emergence and spread of antibiotic-resistant strains of key pathogenic bacteria. since the late 1990s, the problem of antimicrobial resistance has been growing at an alarming rate, generating further clinical, epidemiological, socioeconomic and political problems. an increasing number of patients are susceptible to infections with bacteria that are not normally pathogenic to healthy people and to those in nursing homes, which are important reservoirs of resistance. this is compounded by a decline in interest by pharmaceutical companies in antibiotics that would be effective against multidrug-resistant bacteria. effective treatment and control of common bacterial infections may become increasingly difficult in the future. investing in scientific programmes to develop new antibiotics and new strategies is the most urgent task to be undertaken in the area of countering the phenomenon of increasing drug resistance. a huge neglect is the abandonment of new drug development by pharmaceutical companies over the last 20 years, which has resulted in very high registration requirements, huge clinical trial costs and insufficient industry-wide profits. i want to point out that only two new molecules were introduced into medicine at that time. antimicrobial resistance is not a new phenomenon. the increasing prevalence and emergence of new resistant strains is a serious public health concern. this situation was recognised by the council as early as 1999, when it adopted a resolution on a 'strategy against microbiological threats' and a conclusion on antibiotic resistance. in many countries of the european union, strains of bacteria have emerged that are resistant to all available drugs. the list of pathogens is growing. for these bacteria, new and effective drugs are not expected to be introduced in the near future. the prospect of obtaining them is at least 10 years. infection with drug-resistant bacteria severely limits the availability of proven, safe treatments, requiring the use of so-called last-resort drugs that have increasingly failed in recent times. treatment with these antibiotics is often unscientific and leads to an increase in the number of adverse reactions as well as therapeutic failures. the increase in health care costs for a patient infected with a multidrug-resistant microbe has many dimensions. in addition to the cost of antibiotic therapy itself, there are costs for other medicines used in combination with antibiotics, for transferring the patient to an intensive care unit, and for anti-epidemic measures such as microbiological diagnostics, isolation of patients, and the secondment of staff to care for a single patient. the need for longer hospital stays increases healthcare costs, and the costs of prolonged incapacity for work also increase. since 2001, a great deal of work has been done in the field of antibiotic resistance. i would like to give you a few examples. first, the second commission report on the implementation of the council recommendations on the prudent use of antimicrobials in medicine, published in april 2010, was adopted by the council on 25 june. this report reported on the progress made by member states in the context of the many different initiatives that have been taken since the first report. secondly, the specialised agencies of the european union, in particular the european centre for disease prevention and control, the european medicines agency and the european food safety authority, are working closely together in this area. for example, there are now european-wide networks for monitoring resistance and the use of esac antibiotics in medicine and, to a lesser extent, in veterinary medicine. third, a number of actions have been taken to combat antimicrobial resistance in the food chain. for example, european union legislation on animal nutrition has banned the use of growth-promoting antibiotics in animal feed since january 2006. trends in antimicrobial resistance in animal diseases or infections transmitted from animals to humans and other factors that may pose a risk to public health shall also be monitored. at the international level, the european union supported the adoption of a european strategic action plan on antibiotic resistance at the meeting of the world health organisation regional committee for europe in september this year. we also set up, together with the us, the transatlantic task force on antimicrobial resistance. e council has on several occasions invited member states to take action to ensure the prudent use of authorised antimicrobials in medicine and veterinary medicine. in particular, this concerns the conclusion on antimicrobial resistance adopted in june 2008. in these, the council called on member states to strengthen safety systems and improve the quality of data on antibiotic resistance and antimicrobial use, and to promote the prudent use of antibiotics in both medicine and veterinary medicine. the development of new antimicrobial measures and the important role of incentive schemes for investment in research are issues under consideration by the council. in its conclusions on innovative incentive schemes for effective antibiotics adopted in december 2009, the council called on member states to strengthen incentive schemes for research into and development of new effective antibiotics. it also called on the member states and the commission to enable the development of new antibiotics for which there is a specific medical need, and to identify appropriate regulatory instruments to facilitate the rapid introduction of new antibiotics. ladies and gentlemen! what about the future? all legislative proposals will depend on initiatives by the commission. i am sure that commissioner dalli will be more forthcoming about his plans for the future in this area. the council will naturally give positive consideration to any proposals made by the commission. the issue of antimicrobial resistance will remain a priority for the council. as early as 2009, the council asked the commission to present a comprehensive action plan by the end of 2011 with concrete proposals to encourage the development of new effective antibiotics. we expect to publish this document next month. moreover, the upcoming us-eu summit is also planning to agree on future cooperation in this area. the issue of antibiotic resistance is particularly important from the council's point of view and has therefore been high on the agenda of the danish presidency, our partners in the trio. the danish presidency is planning to organise a conference on the use of antibiotics on 14 and 15 march next year. the conference will address the challenges and risks associated with the use of antibiotics. in conclusion, i would like to say that this assembly intends to adopt a resolution on 'antimicrobial resistance as a public health threat'. it thus follows up on an earlier resolution adopted in may, which focused more on the use of antimicrobials in animals. these initiatives clearly show that the council and the european parliament share the same interest in this issue and have the same objective: to stop the spread of first-line antibiotic-resistant organisms and to develop new effective antibiotics to combat resistant strains. in closing, i would like to express my appreciation and my thanks to you, members of the european parliament, for raising this issue, which is so important for the health of the citizens of the european union.
member of the commission. − mr president, the commission shares the concern expressed in the draft report as regards antimicrobial resistance and has already taken action to address this important threat to health. the commission plans to strengthen action in support of member states in this area and will present, next month, a five-year action plan on antimicrobial resistance (amr). the promotion of the prudent use of antimicrobial agents in human and veterinary medicines will be a cornerstone of our policy and actions for the years to come. the broad aims will be to mitigate the risk of developing amr in humans through promotion of the prudent use of antimicrobials, to help member states address the issue of sales of antibiotics without prescription, to support member states’ enforcement of the prescription-only requirements for antibiotics and to address the identified shortfalls through new activities, such as guidelines, exchange of best practices, etc. for the veterinary sector in particular the issue of amr will be addressed in the context of the review of the legal framework for veterinary medicines and medicated feeding stuffs. as regards the development of new effective antimicrobials, the commission is committed to exploring with all relevant stakeholders how to ensure the availability of new, effective antimicrobials and treatments against infectious diseases, along with the promotion of the prudent use of such antimicrobials. in the context of the current economic difficulties, our joint efforts at local, national and eu level for the prevention and control of antimicrobial resistance across all sectors will also contribute towards mitigating the important economic impact resulting from healthcare costs and productivity losses related to amr.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. mr. president, no one expected fukushima to be hit by a tsunami. hardly anyone foresaw the financial crisis of 2008. our societies are not well prepared for possible, but not common, outlier events. this is particularly true in the case of the creation of antibiotic-resistant microorganisms, where it is a matter of chance or, in the darwinian sense, the evolution of a super-resistant super-microbe that today's antibiotics will not be able to deal with. resistance to antimicrobials is a phenomenon that clearly has a cross-border dimension. the lisbon treaty therefore provides that the european union has the competence and the obligation to act in this area. our defenses in this case are only as strong as its weakest link. we must therefore put particular emphasis on countries with high levels of antimicrobial resistance and it is necessary to address the over-reaction with interventions throughout the chain: citizens, doctors, pharmacists, the pharmaceutical industry. which will have very significant economic and fiscal implications because antibiotics are expensive. it is therefore positive that the principle of precaution is enshrined in our european constitution, the treaty of lisbon. this is because, quite simply, in the history of mankind, we have often had the early signs of an impending catastrophe, but we have not acted in time and the consequences have been dramatic. the case of antibiotics is one such case. we have already seen the first signs and now is the time to act immediately. i am very pleased that the commission is preparing a proposal on how we will act as a european union in concert against this danger and i hope that this proposal will succeed in covering all the important points. we really need to close the door on the unnecessary use of antibiotics. we need to stop giving over-the-counter antibiotics to people, animals and crops.

madam president, in the current economic recession, strengthening the mobility of workers between the countries of the union will make a significant contribution to tackling the employment crisis in terms of the longterm unemployed and those who are high on the unemployment list, but at the same time it will contribute to a more general and more competitive internal market. in this context, it is necessary to modernise the system for the recognition of professional qualifications by linking formal education with non-formal practical learning, after first identifying, assessing and recognising skills in this context. this is a way of helping those from low income groups who for socio-economic reasons have not had the opportunity to study and access the formal education system. i believe that such policies will contribute to growth, to the promotion of knowledge, to combating unemployment and poverty, and to ensuring the social cohesion that we so badly need today.

regulated professions is too high or not high enough, but whether regulation in countries with very many and very strict regulations of these professions is a disproportionate barrier to the proper functioning of the single market. i intend to bring more transparency into this debate by asking all member states to notify all the professions they regulate and to engage in an objective examination
